name: Ego Depletion
description: The (contested) idea that self-control/willpower is a limited resource that depletes with use, making subsequent self-control tasks harder.
design_relevance_note: Often invoked to justify 'reduce the number of decisions users make' design advice — worth real caution given the science below.
myth_risk_note: The foundational work (Baumeister et al.) has 4944 citations while the large registered replication (10.1177/1745691616652873) finding minimal effects has only 1130. The 2016 multi-lab registered replication showed the effect size is much smaller than originally claimed, with confidence intervals including zero. This represents a significant credibility issue where widespread belief in ego depletion substantially exceeds what rigorous replication evidence supports.
prevalence_note: Widely cited in popular psychology and UX writing about decision fatigue, despite the underlying science now being actively contested — a real case worth watching alongside its 'partial' backing_status.

findings.description: A large-scale preregistered replication (23 labs, N≈2,141) of the standard ego-depletion sequential-task paradigm found no significant depletion effect, directly contradicting the original resource-depletion model's central prediction.
findings.source_title: A Multilab Preregistered Replication of the Ego-Depletion Effect

findings.description: Self-control/willpower behaves like a limited resource that depletes with exertion: across four experiments (resisting food temptation, making a meaningful personal choice, suppressing emotion, and an initial self-regulation task), people who exerted self-control on one task subsequently showed reduced persistence/performance on an unrelated second task.
findings.source_title: Ego depletion: Is the active self a limited resource?
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

applications.title: Baumeister et al.'s rejection study: socially excluded participants ate twice as many cookies
applications.description: Researchers Roy F. Baumeister, C. Nathan DeWall, Natalie J. Ciarocco, and Jean M. Twenge (Florida State, Florida Atlantic, and San Diego State universities) told randomly assigned participants either that everyone at a prior social mixer wanted to work with them, or that no one did. Participants were then left alone for 10 minutes with a bowl of 35 mini chocolate-chip cookies under the guise of a taste test. Socially rejected participants ate roughly twice as many cookies, on average, as the socially accepted group -- evidence that social exclusion depletes the self-regulatory resources needed to resist temptation.
applications.ethical_note: This documents a real, peer-reviewed laboratory finding about self-regulation and social rejection, not a persuasion or product-design case -- the deception used in the experiment itself (false peer-feedback) is a standard, disclosed, IRB-reviewed research method, not something being recommended for products.
